objectives: Explain why default credentials are a serious risk in industrial systems
Change the default passwords of the OpenPLC web interface and the FUXA HMI
Describe how login monitoring and access limits complement a strong password
takeaways: Default credentials are published in manuals, so anyone can use them; changing them is the first hardening step.
Harden every account on a system, not only the one a check happens to test.
A long passphrase that is not reused resists the wordlist attacks from the password attack module.
In OT, password changes and lockout policies must not lock operators out of a running plant.
Monitoring failed logins and limiting who can reach a login page add layers beyond the password itself.

checkpoints.question: How does the CybICS check decide that you hardened OpenPLC?
options: It reads OpenPLC's password database
It tries the old default and expects failure
It checks the password length of every user
It asks the IDS whether it saw failed logins
checkpoints.explanation: The check logs in as the default user with the default password. A successful login redirects to the dashboard, so the check fails until the default is refused. It never inspects stored passwords or other accounts, which is why it cannot judge their strength.

quiz.question: You changed the password of the openplc account and the check passed. Is OpenPLC now safe from the dictionary attack you ran earlier?
options: Yes, the check proves no login is weak
Not necessarily, other accounts may be weak
Yes, OpenPLC now locks out repeated guesses
No, the default password still works too
quiz.explanation: The check tests one account. Any other account with a weak password, such as the one you cracked earlier, is still open to guessing, so a real hardening pass reviews every user. Changing the password does not add any lockout.

quiz.question: Which password best resists a wordlist attack?
options: Adm1n2024!
openplc1
five unrelated words
the plant's name in reverse
quiz.explanation: Wordlists contain common passwords and their simple variations, such as swapped letters, added years and symbols, so Adm1n2024! is weaker than it looks. A long passphrase of unrelated words is far outside those lists and still easy to remember.

quiz.question: Why is strict account lockout used carefully in OT systems?
options: PLCs and HMIs cannot count failed logins
It can lock operators out in an emergency
Lockout makes the stored passwords weaker
Locked accounts force a PLC to restart
quiz.explanation: Availability comes first in a plant. Lockout can be abused to deny operators access, or hit an operator during an emergency, so OT often prefers rate limits and alerting instead. Counting failures is easy for any web login.

quiz.question: Which measures help against password guessing on the HMI?
options: Alerting on many logins from one source
Allowing the login only from engineering
One shared admin account for all operators
Slowing responses after failed attempts
quiz.explanation: Alerting, network restrictions and rate limits all make guessing harder or more visible. A shared account may seem easier to protect with one strong password, but it hides who did what and spreads the password widely.

quiz.question: Which MITRE ATT&CK for ICS technique does this hardening defend against most directly?
options: T1694.001 Default Credentials
T0859 Valid Accounts
T0846 Remote System Discovery
T1692.001 Command Message
quiz.explanation: Changing defaults removes the credentials T1694.001 relies on. T0859 Valid Accounts is tempting, but it describes using a working login later; it covers any stolen or guessed password, not specifically the factory default. Discovery and unauthorised commands are stopped by other controls such as firewalls.
